title: How does Kubernetes Service discovery and networking work (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer, kube-dns/CoreDNS, Ingress → Service → Pod), and how do you debug a pod that cannot resolve a Service DNS name?
shortTitle: Kubernetes Service Discovery, Networking, and Debugging DNS Resolution

s1_definition.profdef: Kubernetes Service discovery gives Pods a stable virtual identity in front of ephemeral Pod IPs. A Service of type ClusterIP exposes Pods on an internal virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster, NodePort exposes them on a fixed port of every node, and LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer. CoreDNS resolves Service names like `transfer-service.prod.svc.cluster.local` to the Service's ClusterIP, and an Ingress routes external HTTP by hostname and path to Services, which in turn forward to healthy Pods using their EndpointSlices.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, individual tellers (Pods) come and go and each gets a new desk number (Pod IP) every morning. A Service is the permanent phone extension for the "Transfers department" — you dial the extension, and the switchboard (kube-proxy) connects you to whichever teller is on duty. CoreDNS is the phone directory that turns the department name "transfers" into that extension number. The Ingress is the bank's public reception that reads "I want the loans counter" on a visitor's form and walks them to the right department.
s1_definition.oneliner: Services give Pods a stable virtual IP, CoreDNS maps Service names to that IP, kube-proxy load-balances to Pod endpoints, and Ingress routes external HTTP to Services.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kubernetes Service discovery gives Pods a stable virtual identity in front of ephemeral Pod IPs. A Service of type ClusterIP exposes Pods on an internal virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster, NodePort exposes them on a fixed port of every node, and LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer. CoreDNS resolves Service names like `transfer-service.prod.svc.cluster.local` to the Service's ClusterIP, and an Ingress routes external HTTP by hostname and path to Services, which in turn forward to healthy Pods using their EndpointSlices.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, individual tellers (Pods) come and go and each gets a new desk number (Pod IP) every morning. A Service is the permanent phone extension for the "Transfers department" — you dial the extension, and the switchboard (kube-proxy) connects you to whichever teller is on duty. CoreDNS is the phone directory that turns the department name "transfers" into that extension number. The Ingress is the bank's public reception that reads "I want the loans counter" on a visitor's form and walks them to the right department.

**One line to remember:** Services give Pods a stable virtual IP, CoreDNS maps Service names to that IP, kube-proxy load-balances to Pod endpoints, and Ingress routes external HTTP to Services.

sections.s2_technical:
A ClusterIP Service gets a virtual IP from the Service CIDR. It selects Pods using a label selector, and the EndpointSlice controller keeps a live list of the matching ready Pod IPs. When a Pod sends traffic to the ClusterIP, kube-proxy (via iptables or IPVS rules, or eBPF with Cilium) rewrites the destination to one of the backing Pod IPs. This is why a Service survives Pod churn — the ClusterIP never changes even though Pod IPs do.

NodePort builds on ClusterIP by also opening a port in the 30000–32767 range on every node, so external traffic hitting any node on that port reaches the Service. LoadBalancer builds on NodePort by asking the cloud provider to create an external load balancer that forwards to those node ports, giving a public IP. In practice for HTTP you usually front everything with one Ingress and keep internal Services as ClusterIP.

DNS is central. CoreDNS runs as a Deployment and is itself exposed by a Service (usually named `kube-dns`). Every Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` points at the CoreDNS Service IP and includes search domains like `prod.svc.cluster.local`. So code calling `http://transfer-service:8080` inside namespace `prod` resolves `transfer-service` by appending the search domain to form `transfer-service.prod.svc.cluster.local`, which CoreDNS answers with the Service ClusterIP.

The full external path is Ingress to Service to Pod. An Ingress resource defines host and path rules; the Ingress controller (NGINX, for example) watches them and configures itself to route, say, `api.nbi.com/transfers` to the `transfer-service` ClusterIP, which kube-proxy then load-balances to a ready Pod.

To debug a Pod that cannot resolve a Service name, I work outward layer by layer. First I confirm the name and namespace are right, because a Service in another namespace needs its fully qualified name. Then I exec into the Pod and check `/etc/resolv.conf` to confirm the nameserver is the CoreDNS Service IP and the search domains are present. Next I run `nslookup transfer-service` or use a debug image with `dig`; if that fails I test `nslookup kubernetes.default` to see whether DNS works at all. Then I check that CoreDNS Pods are running and read their logs with `kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns`. I verify the Service exists and has endpoints with `kubectl get endpointslices` — a Service with zero endpoints usually means the selector does not match any ready Pod, often because readiness is failing. Finally I check for a NetworkPolicy that blocks egress to the DNS port 53 or to CoreDNS, which is a very common cause in locked-down banking clusters.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India our Payment API Pod calls the Transfer Service by name. Two real problems drove this scenario.

Problem 1 — Pods restart constantly during deploys, so their IPs change all the time. If the Payment API hardcoded a Pod IP, every deploy would break it. This is exactly what a ClusterIP Service plus CoreDNS solves — the Payment API calls the stable name `transfer-service`, which always resolves to the same virtual IP no matter how many Pods come and go.

Problem 2 — one morning every transfer failed with "UnknownHostException: transfer-service." Nothing was wrong with the Transfer Service itself. The real cause was a new NetworkPolicy that blocked egress to CoreDNS on port 53, so name resolution silently broke. This is exactly why DNS debugging must walk the layers from resolv.conf to CoreDNS to NetworkPolicy.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `ServiceRegistry` that behaves like CoreDNS plus EndpointSlices: it maps a Service name to a ClusterIP and to a set of ready Pod IPs, load-balances across them, and models a DNS failure caused by a blocking NetworkPolicy. A `PaymentClient` resolves `transfer-service` and sends a transfer for Rajesh and Priya, and a `DnsDebugger` walks the diagnostic layers when resolution fails.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the service discovery simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/net/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.net.ServiceDiscoveryDemo

# Real cluster DNS debugging commands
kubectl exec -it payment-pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf            # nameserver + search
kubectl exec -it payment-pod -- nslookup transfer-service        # resolve the name
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=transfer-service
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns                  # CoreDNS logs
kubectl get networkpolicy -n prod                                # check egress to :53
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the Payment API Pod sends a transfer to `transfer-service`, first on a healthy cluster, then after a NetworkPolicy blocks DNS.

Step 1 — The registry is seeded: `transfer-service` maps to ClusterIP 10.96.0.42, which fronts three ready Pod IPs. This mirrors CoreDNS plus an EndpointSlice.

Step 2 — The Payment client resolves `transfer-service` via CoreDNS to 10.96.0.42, then kube-proxy picks the first Pod IP 10.244.1.5. Rajesh is debited fifty thousand rupees and Priya is credited, and the transfer succeeds through that Pod.

Step 3 — A NetworkPolicy is applied that blocks egress to CoreDNS on port 53. The next transfer first tries to resolve the name, but resolution throws an UnknownHostException because DNS egress is blocked. The transfer fails before it ever reaches the Transfer Service.

Step 4 — The DnsDebugger runs the runbook: confirm the fully qualified name, inspect resolv.conf, attempt nslookup (which fails), check that the Service still has endpoints (it does, so the Service is fine), check CoreDNS Pods, and finally find the root cause — the NetworkPolicy blocking port 53. The fix is to add an egress rule allowing UDP and TCP 53 to CoreDNS.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kubernetes Service discovery exists because Pod IPs are ephemeral — Pods are created and destroyed constantly, so nothing should ever talk to a raw Pod IP. A Service gives a stable virtual identity in front of those changing Pods. A ClusterIP Service is reachable only inside the cluster, a NodePort additionally opens a fixed port on every node, and a LoadBalancer provisions an external cloud load balancer for public access. Behind every Service, an EndpointSlice tracks the live list of ready Pod IPs, and kube-proxy, using iptables, IPVS, or eBPF, rewrites traffic from the Service virtual IP to one of those Pods.

Name resolution is handled by CoreDNS, which runs in the cluster and is itself fronted by a Service. Each Pod's resolver configuration points at CoreDNS and carries search domains, so a simple call to a name like transfer-service gets expanded to its fully qualified cluster name and answered with the Service's ClusterIP. For external HTTP, an Ingress sits at the edge and routes by host and path to the right Service, which then load-balances to a Pod, giving the full path of Ingress to Service to Pod.

When a Pod cannot resolve a Service name, I debug outward in layers rather than guessing. I confirm the name and namespace, inspect the Pod's resolver configuration to check the CoreDNS nameserver and search domains, attempt a lookup of both the target and a known-good name like kubernetes.default, verify CoreDNS Pods are healthy and read their logs, confirm the Service actually has endpoints because an empty endpoint list usually means the selector does not match any ready Pod, and finally check for a NetworkPolicy blocking egress to DNS on port 53.

That last cause is exactly what bit us at the National Bank of India. Every transfer suddenly failed with an unknown-host error even though the Transfer Service and its Pods were perfectly healthy. Walking the layers showed the Service still had endpoints, so the service was fine, and the real culprit was a newly applied NetworkPolicy that blocked egress to CoreDNS on port 53. Adding an explicit egress rule allowing UDP and TCP to the DNS port fixed it immediately. The lesson I carry is that in a banking cluster, DNS is a dependency you must explicitly allow in your network policies, and a methodical layer-by-layer check finds the break far faster than restarting Pods at random.
